title: Barabal nic Dhùghaill reads the schedule at Cathair dhearg
summary: A Mission pupil of fifteen, Barabal nic Dhùghaill, renders Lisle's three sealed sheets into Dia-thìris before the council, reading the new fraction twice over at the old custodian of Cnoc bheag's asking. The council has her rendering copied word for word into every coal town's roll, with her own name set at the foot of each copy.

title: The tithe on the tithe named at Dùn fhiadhaich
summary: Griogair Fada, the largest farmer under Cnoc naomh, asks the young tithe-gatherer who set the new weight on grain and gets no answer he can carry home. The custodians of Dùn fhiadhaich enter the weighing in their roll under a name of their own coining, deachamh an deachaimh, the tithe on the tithe.

title: Anne Colby lands at Ros dhomhain
summary: Anne Colby comes ashore at the Ros dhomhain quays at two and twenty, sent out by the Mission with a chest of linen and instruments she has scarcely been shown how to use, hoping to hear word of a brother lost years before on Harrow's ships. She finds no word of him; within the year she finds the flux.

title: Mòr nic Amhlaidh's counsel on names
summary: Washing the chapel floor by lamplight on Colby's first night of nursing the flux, the widow Mòr nic Amhlaidh tells her that the dying want their own names said to them more than they want the fever broken. Colby is said to have kept the counsel from that night on.

title: Colby turns the chapel into a sick-house
summary: Anne Colby has the Mission's chapel at Ros dhomhain opened and its benches carried into the yard without asking anyone's leave, and with Mòr nic Amhlaidh and her daughter carries the flux-sick up from the harbour lodgings on a hand-barrow until the stone room and its yard hold as many as can lie down.

title: The Company's surgeon visits once
summary: The Company's own surgeon comes to the chapel door at Ros dhomhain, will not step past the threshold, and tells Colby she would do better to let the sick lie where they were found. He sends, before he leaves the harbour, a case of salts and does not come again.

title: Colby's roll of the dead by name
summary: Each evening Anne Colby sits at the chapel door with the custodians' own roll open on her knee and a clerk's boy to read her the entries, and sets down against every name who lived and who died, in English, in a column she turns round on the table for the custodians to see is kept.

title: A bargeman put ashore at Seann Vell
summary: A bargeman on the coal run east from Ros dhomhain falls sick at his pole and is put ashore at the Seann Vell landing rather than carried on, the barge-master judging, wrongly, that dry land would serve him better than the water. Within the month the flux is in a dozen houses of the town.

title: Seann Vell shuts its landing
summary: The custodians of Seann Vell, led by Mairead nic Amhlaidh, close the only quay their river town has for the coal traffic that feeds it, and let no barge tie up there through a whole season, though the closing costs the town every fee that quay has ever earned it.

title: The Company fines Seann Vell for the shut landing
summary: A letter from the pay office fines Seann Vell for the season's lost landing fees and says nothing of the flux the closing was meant to check. Mairead nic Amhlaidh reads it to the town council on the landing steps within sight of that season's graves, and the town pays it from the same purse that buried its dead.

title: Arthur Lisle dies at the Residency
summary: Arthur Lisle dies at the Residency above Ros dhomhain of a fever that settles in his chest and then his heart, a fortnight dying by inches and signing papers to the last. He is one and sixty, Commissioner twenty years, remembered by the custodians for a raised voice never once heard at their council table, though not forgiven the schedule.

title: Walter Crane made Commissioner
summary: Walter Crane, six and forty, the Company's chief agent at the pits, takes the Residency's seal within the month of Lisle's death, still in his riding coat from the pit roads. He is the first to hold the Company's office and the Administration's one after the other, and tells the council plainly he sees no sense in the island having two masters where one will serve.

title: The pay office moved to Ceann mhin
summary: Commissioner Crane moves the Company's pay office for the southern workings from the pit-heads to the town of Ceann mhin, so that the crews of every southern pit must walk a day there and a day back, twice a month, to be paid, with no pay given for the two days the walking costs them.

title: Uisdean Ruadh's first walk to Ceann mhin
summary: Uisdean Ruadh, a hewer of Muileann chrom, walks with forty of his gang before light on a morning of frost to stand in the pay line at Ceann mhin till near dusk, and walks home again in the dark. He keeps the cost of it afterward on a notched stick, kept still by his family three generations on.

title: Raghnall Maor dies at Muileann chrom
summary: Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, called Raghnall Maor, dies at two and seventy in the slate-roofed house the Company built him above the pit he first walked as a guide. Anne Colby, sent for by his son, sits with him two nights before the end; he asks her once whether she writes her dead down by name and tells her it is a good thing to keep doing.

title: The Company gives Dòmhnall his father's staff
summary: Within the week of the burying a clerk from Ceann mhin brings Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill the office, the slate roof and the crews together as one paper needing only his mark. The custodians of Muileann chrom, who had hoped the office might die with Raghnall, see it pass from father to son as if it had always been meant to.

title: Raghnall Maor buried beside the eleven
summary: Raghnall Maor is buried on the hill above Muileann chrom beside the eleven of his first gallery, in thin rain, with both shifts of the pit standing at the grave together, a thing not done for any death there before. Anne Colby stands at the grave's edge with her roll and adds, that evening, a line naming his office, the only such line the roll holds.
